parakeet: The real story isn't about monsters under the bed or Santa at the chimney. It's about how a culture teaches children to privilege authority over evidence, to treat superstition as sacred, and to see belief without proof as a virtue. The scaffolding doesn't just shape childhood, it builds the framework for a lifetime of faith. When we step back and look at the full picture, the boogeyman in the shadows, the witch on your back, Santa at Christmas, The Tooth Fairy at night, what we see is not random superstition. We see a system, a system that trains children to fear what they can't see and to hope in what they can't prove, to obey authority over their own senses. In religious homes, this scaffolding feels normal because it's everywhere. Bedtime prayers that focus on death, stories of demons just outside the door, and magical figures who reward belief and obedience. Together, they build a world where the unseen is more real than the seen and where doubt feels like betrayal. But here's the irony. A faith that claims to be anchored in truth relies on the same scaffolding of myth and make believe that secular homes dismantle early. And when children are taught to privilege authority and superstition over curiosity and evidence, we don't just distort their imagination. We limit their potential to explore, to question, to innovate even. That's the difference. In secular homes, imagination and reality reinforce one another. In religious homes, imagination is conscripted into faith, and reality is obscured by it.
